items.title: L11: Matching vetting level to the job
items.source: HMG Personnel Security Controls and National Security Vetting guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: As a manager you often have to say what level of security clearance a post needs. The general principle is that the level follows the access the job genuinely requires, not the grade of the person or the prestige of the team. The Baseline Personnel Security Standard, BPSS, is the pre-employment check that everyone starts with. It is not a national security clearance, but it underpins work with most OFFICIAL material. Above it sit the national security vetting levels. The Counter-Terrorist Check, CTC, is generally for people who need unescorted access to certain sensitive sites or who work in proximity to public figures at risk. Security Check, SC, is generally needed for long-term access to SECRET assets, and for occasional controlled access to TOP SECRET. Developed Vetting, DV, is generally for regular and uninterrupted access to TOP SECRET assets or for certain very sensitive roles. Each level involves more enquiries than the one before it. Two ideas matter for a manager. First, proportionality: asking for more clearance than a post needs wastes time, narrows the pool of candidates and intrudes on people's private lives without good reason. Second, clearance is not a licence. Being cleared to a level does not entitle someone to see everything at that level, because need to know still applies. The decision on clearance is made by the vetting authority on behalf of the department, not by you. Your task is to specify the post's access accurately and then to respect the outcome, including when clearance is delayed or refused.

questions.prompt: A manager wants to attach the highest clearance to a new post 'just to be safe'. What is the main objection?

options.text: A high level makes the post exempt from the baseline checks that apply to everyone else
A high level makes the post exempt from the baseline checks that everyone else completes
The vetting authority can only handle one high-level request per team in any year
Clearance should follow the access the job really needs; excess clearance intrudes and narrows the field

questions.hint: Proportionality means clearance follows genuine access needs, not caution.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits the Baseline Personnel Security Standard?

options.text: A pre-employment check applying to everyone, which is not a national security clearance
The lowest national security clearance, granted after a short interview with security staff
A check used only for people who will handle SECRET assets over a long period
A check that replaces all other vetting once a person has served for several years

questions.hint: BPSS is the starting standard, not a clearance.

questions.prompt: Which role is the closest match for the Counter-Terrorist Check?

options.text: Someone who will have regular access to TOP SECRET assets for many years
Someone who will only read OFFICIAL material at their own desk
Someone who needs unescorted access to certain sensitive sites
Someone who has just joined and wants a title with a security label

questions.hint: CTC is generally linked to site access and proximity to people at risk.

questions.prompt: Someone will have long-term access to SECRET assets. Which vetting level is generally linked to that?

options.text: Baseline Personnel Security Standard
Security Check
Counter-Terrorist Check
Developed Vetting

questions.hint: SC is the usual level for long-term SECRET access.

questions.prompt: Which level generally relates to regular, uninterrupted access to TOP SECRET assets?

options.text: Security Check
Developed Vetting
Counter-Terrorist Check
Baseline Personnel Security Standard

questions.hint: DV is the most thorough level, linked to the highest-level access.

questions.prompt: An EO cleared to SC asks to read a SECRET file belonging to an unrelated team. Which principle decides this?

options.text: Need to know still applies, so clearance alone does not grant access
Clearance at that level gives automatic access to any file at the same classification
The EO may read it provided a manager of any grade is told afterwards
The request is fine because the file is SECRET rather than TOP SECRET

questions.hint: Clearance is necessary but not sufficient; need to know limits access.

questions.prompt: Who takes the decision to grant or refuse a national security clearance?

options.text: The line manager who sponsored the post, after reading the application
The HR business partner, using the candidate's references
The vetting authority acting for the department
The interview panel chair, as a final step before the offer

questions.hint: Managers specify the need but do not decide the outcome.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the vetting levels is generally true?

options.text: All levels involve identical enquiries but differ in how long they last
Developed Vetting is quicker because fewer people are cleared to it
Levels are tied to pay grade, so an SEO always needs DV
Each higher level involves more enquiries than the one below

questions.hint: Higher levels are more thorough and more intrusive.

questions.prompt: A candidate's clearance for a post is refused. What should the hiring manager do?

options.text: Let the person start and work without access until the next review
Respect the outcome and take any questions through HR and security
Ask the vetting team to reverse it because the candidate did well at interview
Share the reasons with the team so that they understand the vacancy

questions.hint: Managers follow the process; they do not override or broadcast it.

questions.prompt: Why does over-specifying clearance cause harm beyond delay?

options.text: It voids the contract of anyone who already holds a lower clearance
It removes the department's duty to complete the baseline checks for the post
It narrows the candidate pool and intrudes on private lives without good reason
It raises the classification of the material the post will handle

questions.hint: Over-specification has real costs for candidates and the organisation.

items.title: L11: A line manager's security duties
items.source: Government Security Classifications and Departmental Security Policy, GOV.UK
items.body: Security is not only the security team's job. A line manager in the Civil Service is the person who turns policy into daily habits for a team. Several duties are common across departments. You should make sure that each person has the right clearance for what they do before they are given access, and that access is removed or changed when a person moves role or leaves, which is often described as joiners, movers and leavers. You should check that your team has completed mandatory security and data protection learning. You should set an example in clear desk habits, locking screens, and handling material according to its classification. You should know who your local security contact is, often called a departmental security officer or similar, and tell your team how to reach them. You should encourage people to report mistakes and near misses promptly, and respond in a way that makes reporting feel safe. Reporting that is punished tends to go quiet. You should also be alert to changes in circumstances: cleared staff are expected to report relevant changes, such as new relationships or financial problems, and you should know where to point them, although you should not pry or decide what the change means yourself. Finally you keep the basic records: who has access to what, which passes and devices were issued, and which have been returned. A manager who is lax about leavers' equipment or about access reviews creates risks that nobody else is placed to see.

questions.prompt: A team member moves to a different directorate. What is the manager's security responsibility?

options.text: Make sure old access is removed or changed to suit the new role
Leave the old access in place in case the person is asked for help later
Wait until the person is cleared for the new role, then ask them to delete files
Pass everything to the new directorate without telling security

questions.hint: Movers should lose access they no longer need.

questions.prompt: When someone leaves the team, which action belongs to the manager?

options.text: Send the person's work files to their personal email for safekeeping
Keep the account active until the end of the financial year
Ask colleagues to share the leaver's login so work continues
Make sure passes, devices and system access are returned or removed

questions.hint: Leavers' equipment and access are a standard manager duty.

questions.prompt: A new starter will handle sensitive material in their first week. What must the manager confirm first?

options.text: That the person has agreed to a shorter notice period in the contract
That the person has clearance matching the access they will be given
That the person has been added to every shared folder by default
That the team has agreed a social event to welcome them

questions.hint: Clearance should match access before access is granted.

questions.prompt: How should a manager respond when a team member admits to a minor security slip?

options.text: Handle the slip quietly in the team so that no record exists
Ask them to fix it first and report only if the fix fails
Treat the report positively and make sure it reaches the right security contact
Issue a formal warning straight away, to deter other staff

questions.hint: Safe reporting encourages more reporting.

questions.prompt: Why is punishing every reported slip likely to backfire?

options.text: People stop reporting, and the department loses early warning of real problems
A legal rule bars disciplinary action for any security error made in good faith
It moves responsibility for the slip from the member of staff to the manager
The vetting authority may withdraw clearance from the whole team as a precaution

questions.hint: Hidden mistakes are more dangerous than reported ones.

questions.prompt: A cleared team member mentions a change in their personal life that may matter to their clearance. What is the best response?

options.text: Decide yourself whether it matters and record your view in your own notes
Tell the rest of the team so everyone can watch for any risk
Advise them to keep it private unless somebody asks directly
Point them to the proper reporting route without judging what it means

questions.hint: Managers signpost; the security process assesses.

questions.prompt: Which is a good example of a manager setting the tone on security?

options.text: Telling the team that the security rules apply to junior staff only
Leaving routine security training until a spare moment arises
Locking their own screen and keeping a clear desk where the team can see
Sharing a login with a trusted colleague to cover absence

questions.hint: Teams copy what their managers do.

questions.prompt: What does 'joiners, movers and leavers' describe?

options.text: Three kinds of probation review used across departments
The categories of staff who need Developed Vetting
The order in which people are told about a reorganisation
The stages at which access to buildings and systems should be set up, changed or removed

questions.hint: It is a process view of access management.

questions.prompt: A manager keeps no record of which devices were issued. What is the main risk?

options.text: Lost or unreturned equipment may go unnoticed, so nobody can report it
Devices become subject to a higher classification automatically after thirty days
The vetting authority will withdraw clearance from all users
Equipment must be returned to the supplier within a week of the loss

questions.hint: Basic records make loss visible.

questions.prompt: Who is the usual first contact for a day-to-day security question in a team?

options.text: The Civil Service Commission, which advises on all security matters
The local security contact, often a departmental security officer
The ICO helpline, which covers every kind of security question
A colleague at the same grade in another department

questions.hint: Know your local contact and tell the team.

items.title: L11: Reporting a security incident
items.source: Government Security Classifications and departmental incident guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: A security incident is any event that puts people, information, systems or premises at risk, or breaks the department's security rules. Examples include a lost laptop or phone, a pass left in a taxi, papers left on a train, an email containing sensitive material sent to the wrong person, a suspicious approach by a stranger asking about your work, a phishing email that you clicked, and a door left propped open. Many incidents are accidental; some are deliberate. The key rule for every incident is to report it quickly, to the right place, and without waiting until you are sure how serious it is. Speed matters because the first hours are when the harm can still be contained: accounts can be locked, devices wiped remotely, and recipients asked to delete a message. Most departments tell staff to report straight away to their line manager and to the security team or a central reporting line, and to follow any instructions they are given. A manager receiving a report should make sure it has reached the security team, note what was said and when, protect the person from blame while the facts are established, and avoid investigating alone. Do not delete evidence, forward the suspicious email widely, or attempt to recover a lost device in a way that creates new risks. You should also avoid describing the incident to people who do not need to know, because that can spread the harm. Afterwards, the focus is on what can be learned and which controls should change.

questions.prompt: A team member clicks a link in a phishing email. What should they do first?

options.text: Wait a few days to see whether anything unusual happens on the device
Delete the email and tell nobody, to avoid alarming colleagues
Report it to security straight away, even if nothing seems to have happened
Forward the email to the whole team as a warning about the new threat

questions.hint: Prompt reporting gives time to contain any harm.

questions.prompt: Why does speed matter when reporting a lost work laptop?

options.text: Delay automatically moves the incident to a higher classification
The loss must be reported to Parliament within a working day
The finder is entitled to keep the device after a fixed period has passed
Accounts can be locked and the device wiped remotely if the report is quick

questions.hint: The first hours are when harm can still be contained.

questions.prompt: An email with sensitive material goes to the wrong person. What is the right approach?

options.text: Report it at once and follow security advice on asking the recipient to delete it
Send a second email telling the recipient to ignore it and say nothing further
Clear your own sent items quietly so that there is no record of the error
Wait to see whether the recipient replies before deciding whether to tell anyone

questions.hint: Report first and do not hide the trail.

questions.prompt: A team member reports an incident to you as their manager. What is the best first action?

options.text: Investigate the cause yourself in detail before you tell anyone else about it
Make sure security has the report, and note the facts as you were told
Decide the severity and report only if you rate it as serious
Ask for a written explanation that stays in the team file

questions.hint: Managers make sure it reaches security rather than investigating alone.

questions.prompt: A stranger at a conference asks detailed questions about your unit's current projects. What does good practice suggest?

options.text: Treat it as a possible suspicious approach and report it
Answer politely, since a conference is a public setting
Ignore it unless the person asks about SECRET work specifically
Wait to see whether the person makes a second approach

questions.hint: Unusual interest in your work is a reportable approach.

questions.prompt: Which action risks making an incident worse?

options.text: Writing down the time and what you noticed
Telling your line manager within minutes
Deleting evidence such as the original suspicious email before security has seen it
Following security's instructions about a lost device

questions.hint: Keep evidence unless told otherwise.

questions.prompt: Which of these is least likely to be treated as a security incident?

options.text: A pass left behind on a public bus after a journey home from work
A secure door propped open for convenience
A laptop stolen from a parked car while the owner was at a meeting
A manager approving annual leave for a team member

questions.hint: Incidents involve risk to people, information, systems or premises.

questions.prompt: Why might it be a mistake to wait until you are sure how serious an incident is?

options.text: Seriousness is decided by the line manager's grade
The facts that make it serious may only be visible to security, and time may be lost
Reports made before certainty are treated as false allegations
A report must include a proposed disciplinary outcome

questions.hint: Report first; assessment comes afterwards.

questions.prompt: After an incident has been contained, where should the emphasis lie?

options.text: Learning what happened and which controls or habits should change
Finding one person to blame so the matter can be closed
Keeping the details from the rest of the team in every case, whatever the lessons
Removing the person's clearance as a routine step after any incident

questions.hint: A learning approach improves security over time.

questions.prompt: A colleague wants to describe an incident in detail to friends in another department. What is the concern?

options.text: It breaches the colleague's contract only if the incident was deliberate
Friends in other departments must always be told within a week
Passing details to people with no need to know can add to the harm
It is acceptable provided no names are used

questions.hint: Incident details are themselves sensitive.

items.title: L11: Data breaches and the first hours
items.source: ICO guidance on personal data breaches; UK GDPR, GOV.UK
items.body: A personal data breach is a security incident that leads to personal data being lost, destroyed, altered, disclosed or accessed without authority. It covers accidental events, such as sending a spreadsheet of people's details to the wrong address, as well as deliberate attacks. Under UK data protection law, organisations must be able to detect, investigate and record breaches. Where a breach is likely to result in a risk to people's rights and freedoms, the organisation must notify the Information Commissioner's Office without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of it. If the breach is likely to result in a high risk to individuals, the organisation must also tell those affected directly. Notice that the 72 hours runs from when the organisation becomes aware, which is why staff must report internally the moment they find a problem. In practice a department has a data protection officer, a privacy or information governance team and a process for deciding whether a breach is reportable. A line manager's role is not to decide on its own whether the ICO is told, but to make sure the internal report is made at once, to contain the problem where it is safe to do so, and to give the specialists the facts: what data, how many people, who might have seen it, and what has been done. Every breach is recorded, even those that are not reported to the ICO, so that patterns can be spotted and controls improved.

questions.prompt: What is the test for something being a personal data breach?

options.text: A criminal attack is carried out by someone outside the organisation
Personal data is lost, altered, disclosed or accessed without authority
More than a stated number of records are lost or exposed in a single incident
The data is published in the press or on social media, causing public concern

questions.hint: Accidents count; the test is loss of control of personal data.

questions.prompt: A spreadsheet of staff details is emailed to the wrong person by mistake. How is this classed?

options.text: Not a breach, because nobody intended any harm
A breach only if the recipient replies
A matter for the recipient rather than the sender's department
As a personal data breach, even though it was accidental

questions.hint: Accidental disclosure is still a breach.

questions.prompt: Under UK data protection law, what is the general timing for telling the ICO about a reportable breach?

options.text: Within 72 hours of the breach happening, whenever it was found
Within a week of the internal investigation closing, once the facts are known
Without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware
Only after every affected person has been contacted and given an explanation

questions.hint: The clock runs from awareness.

questions.prompt: Why must staff report a suspected breach internally at once?

options.text: The ICO fines staff personally for any delay over a day
The 72-hour period runs from when the organisation becomes aware, so delay uses up time
Internal reports are the only way a breach can be recorded
Reports made late are treated as new, separate breaches

questions.hint: Late internal reporting undermines compliance.

questions.prompt: When must affected individuals be told directly?

options.text: Whenever any breach has been reported to the ICO, whatever the level of risk
Never, as telling individuals is a task for the ICO and not the department
Never, as that is the ICO's job
When the breach is likely to result in a high risk to them

questions.hint: High risk to individuals triggers direct notification.

questions.prompt: A manager is told about a breach. Who normally decides whether it is reportable to the ICO?

options.text: The department's data protection and information governance specialists
The line manager of the person who made the mistake
The member of staff who found the error
The most senior member of the affected team

questions.hint: Specialists assess it using the facts the manager supplies.

questions.prompt: Which information is most useful in a manager's internal breach report?

options.text: A view on who is to blame and what penalty the person should receive
The manager's opinion on whether the ICO is likely to be interested
The name of the person who made the mistake, and nothing else at this stage
What data, how many people, who may have seen it and what has been done

questions.hint: Facts enable a quick risk assessment.

questions.prompt: A breach is judged not to need reporting to the ICO. What happens to the record of it?

options.text: It is still recorded internally so patterns can be spotted
It is deleted from the record to protect the staff concerned
It is kept only if a complaint is later received from someone affected
It is sent to the Civil Service Commission instead

questions.hint: All breaches are recorded.

questions.prompt: Which is a sensible containment step for a misdirected email, where it is safe to do so?

options.text: Send the same data again so the recipient has the complete set
Ask the recipient, on specialist advice, to delete it and confirm they have done so
Post a notice about it on the department's public website
Close the sender's account permanently

questions.hint: Containment is about limiting further spread.

questions.prompt: Why should a manager avoid deciding alone that a breach is minor?

options.text: Managers are not permitted to read the data involved
A minor breach cannot be recorded
They may not see the full risk to individuals that a specialist would assess
The ICO must be told of every breach however small

questions.hint: Specialists assess risk consistently.

items.title: L11: Conflicts of interest: spotting and managing them
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code, GOV.UK
items.body: A conflict of interest arises when a personal interest, relationship or outside activity could, or could appear to, influence how you do your public duty. The Civil Service Code requires civil servants to act with integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality, and not to let private interests influence their official work. Conflicts are commonly described as actual, potential or perceived. An actual conflict exists now. A potential one may arise if circumstances change. A perceived one is where an observer might reasonably think your judgement is compromised even if it is not. All three matter, because trust depends on how things look as well as what is true. Typical sources are a family member applying for a job in your team, a friend's company bidding for a contract you help to evaluate, shares in a company affected by a policy, or a role with a charity that receives grants from your department. Having a conflict is not a wrongdoing. Failing to declare it is the problem. The usual steps are to declare it early to your line manager or the person who keeps the register, to agree how it will be managed, and to review it if things change. Management actions include stepping back from a decision, removing someone from a panel, restricting access to papers, or in some cases ending the outside interest. As a manager you also need to look for conflicts in your own team, make declarations a normal topic, and avoid being the person who decides on a matter in which you have an interest.

questions.prompt: What is a 'perceived' conflict of interest?

options.text: A conflict that has been proved by an investigation
A conflict that exists only in an old register
A conflict that concerns only relatives of senior leaders
A situation where an observer might reasonably doubt your impartiality, even if your judgement is sound

questions.hint: Appearance matters because public trust depends on it.

questions.prompt: A friend's company bids for a contract you help to evaluate. What is the right first step?

options.text: Declare it promptly so it can be managed, which may mean stepping back
Evaluate the bid yourself, as long as you score it fairly
Say nothing unless the friend's company happens to win the contract
Ask the friend to withdraw from the process without telling your manager

questions.hint: Declare early; the handling decision belongs to the proper person.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a conflict of interest is correct?

options.text: Having one is a disciplinary offence in itself, whether or not it is declared
Only the most senior grades are expected to declare them in a register
Having one is not wrongdoing, but failing to declare it can be
One declaration is enough, whatever changes in the person's life later

questions.hint: The duty is to declare and manage.

questions.prompt: Which is a typical management action for a declared conflict?

options.text: Deleting the declaration to avoid embarrassment
Removing the person from the panel or decision
Moving the person to a lower grade
Requiring the person to resign in every case

questions.hint: Stepping back is the common remedy.

questions.prompt: A relative applies for a vacancy in your team. What should you do?

options.text: Declare the relationship and take no part in recruiting for that vacancy
Sit on the panel but score your relative last
Advise your relative on how to approach the questions
Wait until your relative is shortlisted before deciding whether to say anything

questions.hint: Remove yourself from the process and declare.

questions.prompt: Why can a conflict still need managing if you are sure your judgement is unaffected?

options.text: The law presumes every personal interest is corrupt
Others cannot see inside your mind, so the appearance of bias can still damage trust
The register is audited by a professional body
Integrity applies only to people who feel conflicted

questions.hint: Public trust relies on appearances as well as facts.

questions.prompt: Which situation is the best example of a potential conflict?

options.text: A declared gift that has already been accepted with approval
A colleague who will retire next year
A shareholding in a company that may be affected by a policy you have not yet begun to work on
A private contract with the department's supplier, already under review

questions.hint: A potential conflict may arise if circumstances develop.

questions.prompt: As a manager, what should you do about your team's declarations?

options.text: Collect them once at induction and not mention them again unless someone raises it
Ask staff to settle declarations privately with the organisation concerned
Keep them out of any register in order to protect each person's privacy
Make them a normal topic and review them periodically, not just at recruitment

questions.hint: Conflicts change over time.

questions.prompt: Who should normally receive a declaration of a conflict?

options.text: The colleague with whom the conflict exists, so they can agree the arrangement
The line manager or whoever keeps the register of interests
Only the recruitment officers in HR, since conflicts arise at recruitment
The department's press office, so that it can prepare lines to take

questions.hint: The line manager or register holder is the usual route.

questions.prompt: A manager has an interest in a matter they must decide. What is the best practice?

options.text: Declare it and ask someone without the interest to decide
Decide it personally and record that the outcome was fair
Delegate to a team member without mentioning the interest
Delay the decision for as long as possible

questions.hint: A person with an interest should not be the decision-maker.

items.title: L11: Gifts and hospitality
items.source: Civil Service Management Code; departmental gifts and hospitality policies, GOV.UK
items.body: Gifts and hospitality are an everyday source of risk, because a small kindness from a supplier or stakeholder can create, or appear to create, an obligation. The Civil Service Code requires you not to accept gifts or hospitality, or receive other benefits from anyone, which might reasonably be seen to compromise your personal judgement or integrity. Departments publish their own detailed policies, which often set thresholds, but the general approach is similar. Declare offers, whether you accept them or not, in the department's register. Very small, token items, such as a branded pen or tea at a meeting, are often allowed without needing approval, although practice varies. Anything more valuable, or from someone with a live commercial interest in a decision, generally needs approval from a manager, and is often declined. Timing matters: an offer from a bidder during a tender is much more serious than the same item at another time. Frequency matters too, because repeated small gifts from one source may add up to a problem. The test to apply is how the offer would look to a reasonable observer. Some gifts cannot be refused without causing offence, for example one handed over at an official visit abroad. In those cases they are usually accepted on behalf of the department and handed in to be recorded. Giving is also covered: you should not offer gifts or hospitality in a way that could be seen as an attempt to influence. Registers are generally open to review, and in some departments published.

questions.prompt: What does the Civil Service Code say about gifts and hospitality?

options.text: Accept any, provided you declare them the next day
Accept those from suppliers but not from members of the public
Do not accept those that might reasonably be seen to compromise your judgement or integrity
Do not accept anything at all in any circumstances

questions.hint: The test is the effect on judgement or integrity.

questions.prompt: A supplier in the middle of a tender invites you to an expensive dinner. What is the best response?

options.text: Accept, provided you pay for your own drinks
Accept, but tell the supplier you will still score fairly
Accept only if the other bidders are invited too
Decline, and record the offer in the register

questions.hint: A bidder's offer during a tender is the most serious case.

questions.prompt: A visiting delegation gives you a gift you cannot refuse without offence. What is usually done?

options.text: Keep it, as it was a personal gesture
Return it by post with a formal letter
Sell it and donate the money to charity
Accept it on behalf of the department and hand it in to be recorded

questions.hint: Official gifts normally belong to the department.

questions.prompt: Which factor makes an otherwise small gift more of a problem?

options.text: The gift being wrapped for presentation
The giver having a live commercial interest in a decision you are involved in
The gift arriving on a weekday
The giver being based outside London

questions.hint: Timing and interest matter.

questions.prompt: Why can frequent small gifts from one source be a concern?

options.text: Together they may build a sense of obligation or the perception of influence
Each must be taxed as income
Small items are illegal if repeated
Frequent gifts are allowed only from public bodies

questions.hint: Cumulative effect matters.

questions.prompt: What is the general rule on declaring offers?

options.text: Declare only gifts you accept
Declare only gifts above the department's threshold when asked
Declare offers whether or not you accept them
Declare only when the giver is a supplier

questions.hint: Declining offers still gets recorded.

questions.prompt: Which statement about giving gifts or hospitality as a civil servant is right?

options.text: Giving is never covered by any policy
Giving is allowed only to ministers
Avoid giving in a way that might be seen as trying to influence someone
Giving is fine if the cost comes from personal funds

questions.hint: The same integrity test applies in both directions.

questions.prompt: A branded pen is offered at a supplier meeting. How do departments commonly treat this?

options.text: Often allowed without approval, though practice varies and policy should be checked
Banned in every department
Allowed only for senior grades
Allowed only if the supplier pays tax on it

questions.hint: Token items are often fine; local policy governs.

questions.prompt: Which question best helps you decide whether to accept an offer?

options.text: Would anyone in the team notice if it went missing?
Could I return the favour later on?
Is the supplier generally pleasant to deal with?
How would this look to a reasonable observer who knew the circumstances?

questions.hint: Appearance to a reasonable outsider is the test.

questions.prompt: Who normally approves acceptance of a more valuable offer?

options.text: The person making the offer
A line manager or other designated person, following departmental policy
A colleague who is a friend of the giver
The finance team, after the event

questions.hint: Approval sits inside your own organisation.

items.title: L11: Outside interests and political activity
items.source: Civil Service Management Code; Civil Service Code, GOV.UK
items.body: Civil servants have private lives, and many have second jobs, voluntary roles, company directorships, rental properties or family businesses. The general rule is that these are allowed unless they conflict with your official duties, damage the reputation of the Civil Service or take up time you owe the department. The practical obligation is to tell your department about outside interests that could cause a conflict, and to seek permission where the rules require it. You should not use official time, premises, equipment or information for outside work. Political activity is governed by the Civil Service Management Code, which divides posts into broad categories: politically free, intermediate and politically restricted. The more senior or sensitive the role, the tighter the limits. Staff in restricted posts are generally not allowed to take part in national political activities, such as standing for Parliament or acting as an officer of a national party, and those in intermediate posts may take part in some activities only with permission. Civil servants in free categories are generally allowed to take part more fully. Even where activity is allowed, you should be careful not to bring politics into your work or to suggest in public that you speak for the department. Civil servants serve the government of the day, whatever its party, and must be seen to do so. If you want to take part in political activity or a public role, ask your line manager or the department's propriety team first, and follow their guidance.

questions.prompt: What is the general approach to a civil servant's outside interests?

options.text: They are banned unless a minister approves
They are allowed only if unpaid
They are allowed unless they conflict with official duties or damage the Civil Service's reputation
They need not be mentioned if outside working hours

options.text: Use their work laptop at first, to keep costs down
Tell the department and seek permission where the rules require it
Mention it only once the business is profitable
Use the office address for customer letters

options.text: Working on the business during a lunch hour away from the desk
Telling a manager about the business
Keeping business papers at home
Using a work email address and laptop for the outside business

questions.hint: Official time, kit and information must not be used.

questions.prompt: Which three broad categories govern political activity under the Civil Service Management Code?

options.text: Politically free, intermediate and politically restricted
Open, limited and closed
National, local and international
Senior, middle and junior

questions.prompt: How do limits on political activity generally vary with the role?

options.text: The more senior or sensitive the role, the tighter the limits
The rules are identical for every role
Junior roles face the tightest limits
Limits apply only to party members

questions.hint: Seniority and sensitivity tighten the rules.

questions.prompt: Which activity is generally not allowed in a politically restricted post?

options.text: Voting in an election
Reading a party's manifesto
Joining a local residents' association
Taking part in national political activities, such as standing for Parliament

questions.hint: Restricted posts are limited in national political activity.

questions.prompt: A civil servant in an intermediate post wants to take part in some political activity. What is usually needed?

options.text: Nothing, because it is a private matter
A letter from the Prime Minister
Permission under the department's rules
A reference from a political party

questions.hint: Intermediate roles typically need permission for some activity.

questions.prompt: Why should civil servants avoid suggesting in public that they speak for the department?

options.text: Departments forbid all use of social media
They serve the government of the day impartially and must keep personal views and official positions apart
Only press officers may hold opinions
Public speaking by civil servants is a criminal offence

questions.prompt: Whom should a civil servant ask before taking up a public role or political activity?

options.text: The party they plan to join
The line manager or the department's propriety team, then follow their guidance
A colleague who has done it before
The local council

questions.hint: Ask inside the department first.

questions.prompt: Which outside role is most likely to attract concern?

options.text: A voluntary role with a charity that receives grants from your department
A voluntary role at a local sports club
A weekend hobby band
Membership of a gym

items.title: L11: The Official Secrets Act and the National Security Act in outline
items.source: Official Secrets Act 1989; National Security Act 2023, legislation.gov.uk
items.body: Two pieces of legislation are central for civil servants who handle sensitive information. The Official Secrets Act 1989 deals mainly with unauthorised disclosure by people who work for the Crown, and by others who have been formally notified that they are subject to it. It covers specific categories of information: security and intelligence, defence, international relations, information that could lead to crime, and certain information obtained from other states or international bodies. For some categories the offence depends on whether the disclosure caused damage. Importantly, the duty continues after you leave the service. Signing a declaration about the Act is a reminder of an obligation that exists in law whether or not you sign. The National Security Act 2023 replaced the older Official Secrets Acts of 1911, 1920 and 1939. It deals with threats from foreign states. It created offences covering espionage, obtaining protected information for a foreign power, assisting a foreign intelligence service, sabotage, and foreign interference, and it updated the law on prohibited places. You do not need to remember the section numbers. A manager should know the practical meaning: classified material is not to be shared with anyone who does not need it and is not authorised; approaches from foreign officials or unfamiliar intermediaries should be reported; and doubts about whether you can say something should be resolved before you speak or publish, not afterwards. Reporting a concern in the proper way is not a breach of the Acts.

questions.prompt: Which best describes the main concern of the Official Secrets Act 1989?

options.text: Regulating how personal data is stored, shared and deleted across public bodies
Setting the pay and grading rules for people employed by departments
Controlling how former ministers lobby their old departments
Unauthorised disclosure of certain categories of information by people who work for the Crown

questions.hint: The 1989 Act concentrates on unauthorised disclosure.

questions.prompt: A civil servant leaves the Service and takes a job in the private sector. What happens to their duty under the 1989 Act?

options.text: It ends on the last day of the notice period, when the contract itself ends
It continues for the first year only, after which it lapses completely
It continues, because the obligation does not end with employment
It ends once the person's security clearance is withdrawn

questions.hint: The duty is lifelong.

questions.prompt: Which kind of information is one of the categories named in the 1989 Act?

options.text: Staff rotas and leave arrangements
Published press releases
Catering and cleaning contracts
Security and intelligence

questions.hint: The Act names specific protected categories.

questions.prompt: Which older legislation did the National Security Act 2023 replace?

options.text: The Official Secrets Act 1989, which was repealed in its entirety
The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998, which protected whistleblowers
The Official Secrets Acts of 1911, 1920 and 1939
The Freedom of Information Act 2000, which governed access to records

questions.hint: The 2023 Act replaced the earlier espionage-era Acts.

questions.prompt: Which conduct falls within the National Security Act 2023?

options.text: Espionage, sabotage and foreign interference
Late payment of supplier invoices
Late payment of supplier invoices and other breaches of procurement rules
Breaches of the department's dress code and attendance requirements

questions.hint: It addresses threats from foreign states.

questions.prompt: A foreign official you have just met at an event asks, in a friendly way, about your department's plans. What should a manager advise?

options.text: Answer if the plans are only classified OFFICIAL, since the risk is low
Report the approach to security, even if the conversation seemed harmless
Wait to see whether a second approach is made before telling anyone
Ask the official to put the request in writing and then reply formally yourself

questions.hint: Unusual approaches should be reported early.

questions.prompt: You are unsure whether you may talk about a project at a public event. What is the right course?

options.text: Check with the people responsible before speaking or publishing anything
Speak in general terms and check afterwards if anyone objects
Leave out the department's name and then say what you like about the work
Ask a friend in another department what they would do

questions.hint: Resolve doubts before, not after.

questions.prompt: What does signing a declaration about the Official Secrets Act do?

options.text: It creates the legal obligation for the first time on signature
It gives immunity from prosecution for disclosures made in good faith
It applies the obligation only for as long as the job lasts
It reminds you of an obligation that already exists in law

questions.hint: The duty exists whether or not you sign.

questions.prompt: Which statement about reporting a security concern through the proper route is correct?

options.text: It is treated as a breach if the concern later turns out to be unfounded
Reporting properly is part of the system and is not itself a breach
It is a breach unless a lawyer has approved the report first
It is treated as a breach unless it is made in writing and signed by the reporter

questions.hint: Proper reporting is the intended route.

questions.prompt: Which is the best summary of the practical lesson for a manager?

options.text: Share widely inside the department so that any errors are spotted early
Treat every piece of information as classified, whatever its content
Never share classified material with anyone not authorised and with no need for it
Leave all questions about the Acts to the press office to settle

questions.hint: Authorisation and need to know are the daily test.

items.title: L11: Raising concerns under the Civil Service Code
items.source: Civil Service Code; Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998, GOV.UK
items.body: The Civil Service Code sets out what civil servants should do if they are asked to act in a way that conflicts with the Code, or if they see others doing so. If you become aware of actions that are illegal, improper, unethical, in breach of constitutional convention or professional codes, or that are inconsistent with the Code, you should report the matter in accordance with the relevant procedures. Normally this means raising it with your line manager or someone in your management chain. Departments also have nominated officers who can hear concerns in confidence and give advice, and there may be a confidential helpline. If you have raised a concern through those routes and you do not believe it has been properly addressed, or if the concern is serious and you do not feel you can use them, you may take it to the Civil Service Commission, which is independent of departments. The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 gives legal protection to workers who make a protected disclosure, which can protect against dismissal or unfair treatment for raising a concern in the right way. This is why the route matters: going first to the press may reduce protection and might, if secret information is involved, break other laws. As a manager, you have extra duties. You must take a concern seriously, record it, pass it to the right place if you cannot deal with it yourself, protect the person raising it from detriment, and never try to find out or reveal their identity unless necessary and agreed.

questions.prompt: A civil servant is asked to do something they believe is improper. What does the Civil Service Code expect them to do?

options.text: Raise it through the relevant procedures
Wait to see whether the request is repeated before acting
Refuse in public and tell the team why
Comply, and keep a private note in case it matters later

questions.hint: The Code requires reporting through proper routes.

questions.prompt: Which is the usual first route for raising a concern about conduct?

options.text: A journalist who has covered the department before
A colleague in another department with more experience
A line manager or someone in your management chain
An MP who sits on a relevant committee

questions.hint: Internal routes normally come first.

questions.prompt: What is a nominated officer?

options.text: A senior official who nominates staff for honours and awards
A person in the department who hears concerns in confidence and gives advice
A member of the Civil Service Commission who hears appeals
A union representative appointed by the department

questions.hint: Nominated officers provide confidential support.

questions.prompt: When may a civil servant take a concern to the Civil Service Commission?

options.text: Only once they have left the Civil Service
At any time, in preference to the internal routes
Only if a permanent secretary agrees to the referral
If it has not been properly dealt with internally, or the internal routes cannot be used

questions.hint: The Commission is the independent route.

questions.prompt: What does the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 provide?

options.text: Immunity from any consequence of any disclosure made to any person
Legal protection for workers who make a protected disclosure in the right way
A financial reward for people who report wrongdoing
A duty on every worker to report suspected wrongdoing to the police

questions.hint: PIDA protects against detriment.

questions.prompt: Why might going first to the press be a poor choice?

options.text: The press are legally unable to publish anything provided by a civil servant
Civil servants are forbidden by the Code from reading or commenting on the news
It may reduce legal protection and could break laws on secret information
It makes the matter more confidential than an internal report

questions.hint: The route affects protection.

questions.prompt: A staff member brings you a concern about a colleague's conduct. What should you do first?

options.text: Advise them to wait a month and see whether the behaviour happens again
Raise it directly with the colleague concerned that same day
Share it with the team to see whether anyone else has noticed the same thing
Take it seriously, listen carefully and record what is said

questions.hint: A manager's first duty is to listen and record.

questions.prompt: How should a manager treat the identity of a person who raises a concern?

options.text: Protect it, and do not try to find out or reveal it unless necessary and agreed
Tell the person concerned, so that they can reply fully
Record it in the team's shared drive so that others can support them
Reveal it to anyone senior who asks for it, since seniority brings the right to know

questions.hint: Confidentiality protects the person raising the concern.

questions.prompt: What does 'detriment' mean in the context of raising concerns?

options.text: A payment made to settle a complaint
Unfair treatment of someone because they raised a concern
A change of desk after a team move
A delay in dealing with a concern

questions.hint: Protection from detriment is central to PIDA.

questions.prompt: A manager receives a concern that falls outside their remit. What is best practice?

options.text: Hold it until the next performance review is due
Handle it quietly alone, without telling anyone else
Pass it to the right place and tell the person what will happen next
Tell the person it is not really a concern

questions.hint: Referral to the proper channel is part of the duty.

items.title: L11: Inducting a new starter
items.source: Civil Service induction guidance; Civil Service Code, GOV.UK
items.body: Induction is where a new starter's understanding of the Civil Service Code, security and ways of working begins, and a manager owns much of it. A good induction starts before day one: confirm that checks are complete, set up access that matches the clearance, order equipment and tell the team that someone is arriving. On day one, welcome the person, explain the building and passes, introduce the team and give a clear picture of the first weeks. Security induction normally includes the basics of classification, clear desk, reporting incidents and the rules for working remotely, together with mandatory learning on data protection, security, equality and the Civil Service Code. New staff should be told who their local security contact is, how to report an incident and how to raise a concern. They should be asked to declare any outside interests or relationships that could conflict with the role, and told where policies are kept. Reasonable adjustments agreed during recruitment must be in place from the start, because the Equality Act applies from day one. Plan the first weeks: set early objectives, arrange regular one-to-ones, and give a buddy if you can. Check in on how the person is settling as well as what they are producing. If you have people joining who are working remotely, think about how they will meet the team and how you will notice if something is wrong. A well-run induction reduces errors, including security errors, and sets the tone for probation.

questions.prompt: Which of these should happen before a new starter's first day?

options.text: Full access to all shared drives is granted, to save time later
Equipment orders are held back until the end of the new starter's first week
Objectives are left open until the person asks about them
Checks are confirmed complete and access is set up to match their clearance

questions.hint: Preparation includes checks and matching access.

questions.prompt: Which is a sensible part of a security induction?

options.text: How classification works, clear desk habits, incident reporting and remote working rules
How the department's pay scales are negotiated each year
How planning applications are processed by councils
How to deal with press enquiries about security matters

questions.hint: Security induction covers practical basics.

questions.prompt: What should new starters be told about security contacts?

options.text: That security questions should wait until after the probation period has finished
That any security concern should go straight to the department's press office
That the reception desk deals with every security matter on the department's behalf
Who the local security contact is and how to report an incident

questions.hint: People need the route from the start.

questions.prompt: Why must agreed reasonable adjustments be in place from the first day?

options.text: Adjustments are optional until the person has passed probation
The Act applies only after a year of service
The Equality Act applies from day one, not after probation
Adjustments are the new starter's own responsibility to arrange

questions.hint: Legal duties apply from the start.

questions.prompt: How should outside interests be handled at induction?

options.text: New starters are asked to declare any that might conflict, and shown where policies are kept
They are left until the first appraisal, when they can be raised
They are discussed only with staff who will join a senior team
They are recorded only if the new starter volunteers them

questions.hint: Early declarations avoid later problems.

questions.prompt: Which practice helps a new remote starter most?

options.text: Leaving them to introduce themselves in whatever way they choose
Planning how they will meet the team and how you will notice if something is wrong
Waiting for them to raise any problems themselves
Delaying objectives until they can attend the office in person

questions.hint: Remote starters need deliberate contact.

questions.prompt: What is the main value of regular one-to-ones in the first weeks?

options.text: They count as the formal probation reviews on their own
They help the person settle and give early chances to spot problems
They are mostly needed for staff whose early performance has caused concern
They replace the need to complete the mandatory learning modules

questions.hint: Regular contact supports settling in.

questions.prompt: Which induction practice is poor?

options.text: Pairing the person with a buddy for the first weeks
Explaining how to report an incident or a concern
Setting early objectives and agreeing how they will be reviewed
Giving full system access on day one without checking clearance

questions.hint: Access must match clearance.

questions.prompt: How does a good induction help probation?

options.text: It makes later probation reviews unnecessary
It removes the need to set objectives
It sets out expectations, so probation is fair and clear
It allows feedback to be left until the end of probation

questions.hint: Clear expectations support fair probation.

questions.prompt: Which mandatory learning is typical for new starters?

options.text: Data protection, security, equality and the Civil Service Code
Advanced statistics and modelling, completed at practitioner level
A specialist legal qualification, awarded after a formal examination
Project management certification at practitioner level

questions.hint: Mandatory learning covers core obligations.

items.title: L11: Probation: the manager's role
items.source: Civil Service Management Code; departmental probation guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: Probation is a period at the start of a role when a manager assesses whether the person is suitable for it and gives them the chance to settle and improve. Its length and rules are set in the contract and departmental policy, so check what applies to your staff rather than assuming. The manager's duties follow a pattern. First, set clear expectations at the start: objectives, standards of behaviour, and how performance will be judged. Second, hold regular conversations and record them, so that nothing in a formal review is a surprise. Third, give feedback early and honestly, praising what is going well and naming gaps in specific terms. Fourth, offer support: training, a buddy, adjustments, and time. Fifth, if there are concerns, act promptly rather than leaving them until the end, because a problem that is raised late is both unfair to the person and weak as a record. If performance or conduct is a concern, follow the department's procedure: a written warning of the problem, a reasonable chance to improve, and a review. Probation does not remove the person's protection against discrimination, and the Equality Act applies throughout. Some concerns, such as a security breach, may need a different route as well, and should go to HR and security. Keep notes factual and avoid opinions. At the end, make a decision based on the evidence, tell the person promptly and confirm it in writing. Do not use probation as a way to avoid a difficult conversation or as a shortcut around fair process.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of probation?

options.text: To test whether the person will accept a lower salary after a trial
To delay the issue of a contract until performance is proven
To assess suitability for the role while giving the person a chance to settle and improve
To replace the pre-employment checks with an observation period

questions.hint: It is a supported assessment period.

questions.prompt: What should a manager do at the start of probation?

options.text: Wait until problems appear before explaining what is expected
Tell the person informally that the first month does not count
Hold back feedback to avoid putting pressure on them
Set clear objectives and standards of behaviour

questions.hint: Clear expectations come first.

questions.prompt: Why should regular probation conversations be recorded?

options.text: Because the notes must be read aloud at each review meeting
So that formal reviews hold no surprises and the record is fair
So that they can be published to the wider team after each meeting
So that they replace the need to give feedback in person

questions.hint: Records support fairness.

questions.prompt: A manager notices a performance problem in week three. What is the best course?

options.text: Raise it promptly and offer support and a chance to improve
Wait until the final review so the whole picture is clear
Mention it to the rest of the team first so that they can offer help
Wait to see whether it fades as the person gains experience of the role

questions.hint: Early action is fairer and gives better evidence.

questions.prompt: What should notes about a probationer's performance contain?

options.text: The manager's guesses about the person's attitude
Comparisons with how colleagues behave outside work
Facts and specific examples
General impressions of how the person fits in

questions.hint: Keep records factual.

questions.prompt: A probationer says they were treated unfairly because of a protected characteristic. What is correct?

options.text: The Act only applies once probation has been formally passed
The Equality Act applies throughout, including during probation
The Act applies only to those on fixed-term contracts
The Act applies only after the person's first appraisal

questions.hint: The Act applies from day one.

questions.prompt: A probationer commits a security breach. What is a sensible approach?

options.text: Report it through security channels as well as considering the probation process
Keep it in the probation file only
Leave it until the end of probation
Discuss it in a team meeting as a lesson

questions.hint: Security issues need the right route.

questions.prompt: How should a manager find out how long probation lasts for their staff?

options.text: Assume it matches whatever the department used for its last intake
Decide it individually for each person on how quickly they seem to settle
Leave it open until performance is clear
Check the contract and departmental policy

questions.hint: It is set by contract and policy.

questions.prompt: At the end of probation, what is the right approach to the decision?

options.text: Decide on instinct and inform the person informally
Delay telling the person until they ask
Base it on evidence, tell the person promptly and confirm in writing
Let the team vote on whether to confirm

questions.hint: Decisions need evidence and clarity.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a misuse of probation?

options.text: Using it to avoid a difficult conversation or as a shortcut around fair process
Setting objectives at the start
Offering a buddy and training
Recording one-to-ones and sharing the notes with the person

questions.hint: Probation must follow fair process.

items.title: L11: Employment checks when you recruit
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard; Civil Service Recruitment Principles, GOV.UK
items.body: When you recruit, you are responsible for making sure the process is fair and that the checks match the role. Civil Service appointments are made on merit, on the basis of fair and open competition, as set out in the Recruitment Principles. The pre-employment checks for most roles follow the Baseline Personnel Security Standard, which verifies identity, confirms the right to work in the UK, checks employment history, usually for the past three years, and asks about unspent criminal convictions. Some posts also have nationality requirements, set out in the advert, and some need higher national security vetting or other checks, such as a Disclosure and Barring Service check where the work involves vulnerable people. Checks should be proportionate and applied consistently to all candidates for the same role. The offer is conditional on satisfactory completion, so the candidate should be told clearly what is needed and by when. In accordance with the Equality Act, you should not ask about a candidate's health before making an offer, except in narrow circumstances such as arranging adjustments for the selection process or checking whether someone can do a function essential to the job. Declared convictions are considered for their relevance to the role, not automatically fatal. If evidence from checks does not match what a candidate said, discuss it with HR rather than deciding alone. Keep records of decisions and protect candidates' data. Do not allow a person to start work with access until the checks that the role requires are done, unless the department's policy allows interim arrangements.

questions.prompt: On what basis are Civil Service appointments generally made?

options.text: On the seniority of the applicant's last employer
On recommendation from a senior official
On the order in which applications arrive
On merit, following fair and open competition

questions.hint: The Recruitment Principles require merit and fair competition.

questions.prompt: Which set of checks forms the Baseline Personnel Security Standard?

options.text: Credit history, social media history and references from friends
Identity, right to work, employment history and unspent convictions
A full medical examination and a check on the candidate's driving record
Ten years of references from every previous employer the candidate has had

questions.hint: BPSS has four elements.

questions.prompt: When might a Disclosure and Barring Service check be needed?

options.text: For every post in the Civil Service, whatever the nature of the work
Only for people who hold a driving licence and travel for work
Where the work involves vulnerable people
Only for posts at Grade 7 and above in the public-facing departments

questions.hint: DBS checks are linked to the role.

questions.prompt: Why should checks be applied consistently to all candidates for a role?

options.text: It lets the department keep requirements confidential
It removes the need to keep records of decisions
It speeds up the process by reducing the number of checks
It is fair, proportionate and avoids discrimination

questions.hint: Consistency supports fairness.

questions.prompt: What does the Equality Act generally say about health questions before an offer?

options.text: Do not ask, except in narrow circumstances such as arranging adjustments
Ask every candidate to complete a full health form
Ask only candidates who mention a disability
Ask only candidates for senior posts

questions.hint: Pre-offer health enquiries are restricted.

questions.prompt: A declared conviction appears on a candidate's form. What is the right approach?

options.text: Reject the candidate automatically on that ground
Consider it for relevance to the role, following the department's process
Ignore it, as the conviction was in the past
Share it with the rest of the team to get a view

questions.hint: Declared convictions are weighed for relevance.

questions.prompt: Evidence from checks does not match what a candidate said. What should the manager do?

options.text: Withdraw the offer immediately, without contacting anyone
Discuss it with HR before reaching a decision
Treat it as a clerical issue and ignore it
Ask referees to confirm it informally

questions.hint: A mismatch needs a fair, joined-up process.

questions.prompt: Why is a job offer described as conditional?

options.text: It depends on the checks being completed satisfactorily
It depends on the candidate accepting within a day
It is not binding on the department in any circumstances
It lasts only for the first week of employment

questions.hint: Conditional means subject to checks.

questions.prompt: Where would a nationality requirement normally be stated?

options.text: Only at interview
In the induction pack
On the contract after signature
In the job advert

questions.hint: Adverts set out requirements.

questions.prompt: How should a manager handle candidate data collected during checks?

options.text: Share it with anyone who asks for it
Leave it on a shared drive so the panel can see it
Keep records of decisions and protect the data in line with data protection rules
Delete the decision notes at once to protect candidates

questions.hint: Data protection applies to checks.
